newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan's new history texts revive dispute over war.
newsitem.headline: Japan's new history texts revive dispute over war.

text.p: Japanese students started a new school year on Monday which once again was marked by the seemingly endless controversy about how textbooks should portray the nation's World War Two actions.
The latest flashpoint is a new reference in junior high school history textbooks to the Japanese army's use of sex slaves during the war.
The debate is over whether "comfort women" - the euphemism for 200,000 Asian women historians estimate worked in frontline brothels for Japan's Imperial Army -- were forcibly recruited.
But the dispute has raised broader questions about Japan's identity, its place in a resurgent Asia and the way its foreign and defence policies are formed.

The debate has similiarities to a 1982 row when censorship of history textbooks by Japan's Education Ministry angered China, South Korea and other Asian nations by describing Japan's World War Two invasion of the region an "advance".
This time, however, the ministry -- which later backed down in the face of Asian complaints -- is under fire from the Japanese right for going too far in depicting the past.
In the view of conservatives and nationalists, Japan is trapped in a "masochist" view of history, amplified by decades of scholarship dominated by Marxist academics.
They say patriotism has become a dirty word and created a pacifist country unable to prepare for crises or debate security interests for fear of offending China and the Koreas.
Liberals and leftists counter that without a forthright examination of its history, Japan -- if not doomed to repeat the tragedy -- will be unable to coexist with its neighbours.

On the sex slave issue, the nationalist camp argues that there is no conclusive evidence the women were abducted by the army. They say the military's role was limited to brothel logistics such as hygiene and transportation.

Teaching junior high school students -- those aged 13 to 15 years of age -- about comfort women would make "many students say they are ashamed to be Japanese and wish they were not born in their country," the conservative daily newspaper Sankei Shimbun said in a recent editorial.

Liberals and left-leaning scholars argue the government itself has admitted "in many cases" the women were recruited against their will in a programme in which military and administrative authorities were directly involved.

The August 1993 admission by the cabinet of then prime minister Kiichi Miyazawa ended years of official denial and formed the basis of the Education Ministry's approval of the use of textbooks which refer to the comfort women.
"The government and military's deep involvement is clear," said a large headline in the liberal newspaper Asahi Shimbun.

Determined to win the war even if they have lost the latest battle over World War Two, a group of conservative scholars has launched an effort to write a new history textbook which they say will do a better job of instilling national pride.
Author Naoki Inose, whose works include detailed examinations of modern history, says both pacifists and nationalists miss a key point about the war's lessons.
"Both sides overlook the continuity between the pre-war political system which brought about that tragedy and the post-war ways of often unaccountable governments," he said.

"In both situations, there was a political black hole at the centre which offered no guidance or values while virtually autonomous groups -- the wartime army or modern ministries -- pursued their own interests," he said in an interview.
